blocks.text: Although most browsers allow exporting HTTP headers with or without data to a .har file, Fiddler typically saves them to a .saz file.
You can install Fiddler from the official website and then import either the .har or the .saz file to review the HTTP headers.
If you do not want to install Fiddler, you can use one of the following approaches to analyze HAR files within a browser such as Google Chrome.
You can import the HAR file directly in your browser developer tools as shown in the following image.
You can use the free web-based HAR analyzer tool in the Google Admin Toolbox.

blocks.item: To review the HAR file in the Google HAR analyzer after the file is uploaded, review the list of the requests on the left, which can be filtered by code (e.g., 2xx, 3xx, 4xx, or via search).
If you select a specific request, you can see details on the right:
The destination URL of the request.
This helps you determine whether the request is proxied through the Zscaler service (generally, the response is HTTP 1.1 unless the organization enabled and configured H2).
Alternatively, if you know H2 is configured for the domain, it can help confirm that HTTP2 is being used.
If this is Tunnel 1/Explicit Proxy, you can also look at the remote address to check whether it is a Proxy VIP.
Request method (GET, POST). For POST requests, you can see the request payload on the Post Data tab. For both GET and POST requests, you can view the response body on the Response Content tab.
The remote IP. This identifies which node a request is landing on. However, the Zscaler admin portals are now behind cloudfront CDN, so the IP is from AWS.
